Incircle In Segment

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a small circle sits in a big circle, touching a straight chord and the big circle.
How to play: Drag point A, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to move the chord. Tick the box for the proof lines and press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

Move the touching point A and the little circle changes size and position. Yet the line through its two touching points always passes through the same bottom point of the big circle. That point is the midpoint of the arc on the other side of the chord.

One line through three points

The claim on the original page is exact: a chord ST cuts a circle with centre O. A circle inside the circular segment touches the chord at A and the outer circle at B. If M is the midpoint of the arc cut off by ST that does not contain B, then A, B and M lie on one line. The logic test checked this, and the tangency and arc-midpoint facts, at every one of 500-plus positions of A; the largest departure was less than a billionth of a board unit.

Why the chord stays flat

The applet keeps M at the bottom of the circle. An inversion centred at M that swaps A with B turns the outer circle into the chord: a line parallel to the tangent at M, hence horizontal. If h = M.y - A.y and q = MA², the ray MA meets the circle again at B, scaled by 2R h / q. The small circle then has radius rho = R(1 - q/(2Rh)), centre rho above A, and it is tangent to both circles. It is largest, with radius R/2, when A is the centre.

Two short proofs

Let O' be the small centre. The triangle AO'B is isosceles because O'A = O'B = rho. Extend AB past A to meet the line OM at N: triangles AO'B and NOB share the angle at B, and ON is parallel to O'A, so NOB is isosceles too and OB = ON = R. That forces N = M. Or, in the language of homothety, the two circles are homothetic with centre B; the lowest point of the small circle maps to the lowest point of the big one, which is M. Corresponding points of a homothety line up with its centre.

From the old applet

This is the single-circle theorem. Its sibling Incircle In Segment 1 draws two circles in the same segment and claims that their common chord, the radical axis, passes through M, using MA × MB = MT². Here the Java applet draws the inscribed circle by inversion, paints the inverted circle and the extended chord, and offers a Hint checkbox. The Java page has that checkbox twice because of a copied panel; this page shows it once. A starts at a fixed spot instead of a random one and is kept inside the disc, where the inscribed circle really exists; M stays fixed at the bottom as it does on this page. Colours and the SVG replace the applet's magenta, blue and dark green.

Try putting A exactly at the centre: the chord through it is a diameter, and the small circle reaches half the big radius.
